{{Short description|Theorem in statistics regarding the Likelihood Principle}}

'''Birnbaum's Theorem''' is a pivotal result in the [[foundations of statistics]], formulated by the American statistician [[Allan Birnbaum]] in 1962. The theorem formally demonstrates that the [[likelihood principle]] is logically equivalent to the combination of two more widely accepted statistical principles: the [[sufficiency principle]] and the [[conditionality principle]].

The publication of the theorem in the ''[[Journal of the American Statistical Association]]'' was a landmark event that sparked intense debate between [[Frequentist inference|frequentist]] and [[Bayesian inference|Bayesian]] statisticians, as the likelihood principle implies that many standard frequentist methods (such as [[p-value]]s and [[confidence interval]]s) violate basic axioms of consistency.<ref name="Birnbaum1962">{{cite journal |last1=Birnbaum |first1=Allan |title=On the Foundations of Statistical Inference |journal=Journal of the American Statistical Association |date=1962 |volume=57 |issue=298 |pages=269–306 |doi=10.1080/01621459.1962.10480660 |url=https://www.tandfonline.com/doi/abs/10.1080/01621459.1962.10480660|url-access=subscription }}</ref>

==Definitions and principles==
Birnbaum's theorem concerns the "evidential meaning" of an [[experiment]], denoted as <math>\text{Ev}(E, x)</math>, where <math>E</math> is the experiment and <math>x</math> is the observed data.

===Sufficiency principle (S)===
The sufficiency principle states that if <math>T(x)</math> is a [[sufficient statistic]] for a parameter <math>\theta</math>, then the evidential meaning of the data <math>x</math> is the same as the evidential meaning of the statistic <math>T(x)</math>. Formally:
:<math>
\text{Ev}(E, x) = \text{Ev}(E, T(x))</math>
This principle is widely accepted by almost all statistical schools of thought.

===Conditionality principle (C)===
The conditionality principle states that if an experiment is chosen by a random mechanism (such as a [[coin flip]]) that does not depend on the parameter <math>\theta</math>, then the evidence provided by the result depends only on the experiment actually performed. For example, if a researcher decides to perform either experiment <math>E_1</math> or <math>E_2</math> based on a fair coin toss, and <math>E_1</math> is chosen, the evidence <math>\text{Ev}</math> should not be affected by the fact that <math>E_2</math> "could have" been performed.

===Likelihood principle (L)===
The likelihood principle states that all the [[information]] about <math>\theta</math> from an experiment is contained in the [[likelihood function]] <math>L(\theta) = f(x\mid \theta)</math>. Two different experiments yielding the same likelihood function (up to a multiplicative constant) should result in the same inference about <math>\theta</math>.

==The theorem==
Birnbaum's theorem states:
<blockquote>
The likelihood principle (L) is equivalent to the conjunction of the sufficiency principle (S) and the conditionality principle (C).
</blockquote>
Symbolically:
:<math>
(S \text{ and } C) \iff L</math>

===Significance===
While (S) is viewed as intuitively obvious by many statisticians, there are severe reservations about the suitability of (C), in particular with the equivalence format used in (C). By 1969, Birnbaum had rejected both his (C) and the likelihood principle (L). (L) implies that the [[stopping rule]] of an experiment (for example, whether a researcher decided to stop after 10 trials or after seeing 3 successes) should not affect the final inference{{mdash}}a direct contradiction to how p-values are calculated.<ref name="BergerWolpert">{{cite book |last1=Berger |first1=James O. |last2=Wolpert |first2=Robert L. |title=The Likelihood Principle |date=1988 |publisher=Institute of Mathematical Statistics |isbn=978-0940600133 |url=https://projecteuclid.org/ebooks/ims-lecture-notes-monograph-series/The-Likelihood-Principle/toc/10.1214/lnms/1215466210}}</ref>

==Criticisms==
Following Birnbaum's original paper, several statisticians challenged the proof.
* [[Deborah Mayo]] argued in 2004 that Birnbaum's application of the conditionality principle was flawed because it assumes the existence of an "evidential" framework that may not be compatible with frequentist goals of [[Type I and type II errors|error control]].<ref name="Mayo2010">{{cite book |editor1=Taper, Mark L. | editor2=Lele, Subhash R.|last=Mayo | pages=79–118|first=Deborah G. |publisher=University of Chicago Press|title=The Nature of Scientific Evidence: Statistical, Philosophical, and Empirical Considerations |date=2004 |chapter=An Error-Statistical Philosophy of Evidence (Chapter 4)|url=https://doi.org/10.7208/chicago/9780226789583.001.0001 |access-date=2025-12-19 |doi=10.7208/chicago/9780226789583.001.0001|isbn = 9780226789552}}</ref>
* [[Michael Evans (statistician)|Michael Evans]] and others have revisited the proof using different categorical frameworks, generally upholding Birmbaum's logic while noting that the "evidence" <math>\text{Ev}</math> must be carefully defined to avoid mathematical trivialities.<ref name="Evans1">{{cite journal |last1=Evans |first1=Michael |last2=Fraser |first2=D. A. S. |last3=Monette |first3=Georges |title=On Principles and Arguments to Likelihood |journal=The Canadian Journal of Statistics |date=1986 |volume=14 |issue=3 |pages=181–194 |doi=10.2307/3314794|url=https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/10.2307/3314794|publisher=Statistical Society of Canada|url-access=subscription }}</ref>
